**Monday, August 24, 1931**

The date carries a long history of its own. On August 24, 79 AD — 1,852 years before you were born — Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried Pompeii under volcanic ash, preserving an entire Roman city in its final moment. The younger Pliny, watching from across the bay, wrote the first eyewitness account of a volcanic eruption in recorded history. On August 24, 1572 — 359 years before your birth — the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre began at dawn in Paris, as French Catholics killed thousands of Protestant Huguenots in an outbreak of religious violence that shocked even a Europe accustomed to religious war. Your birthday is one of history's recurring appointments.

The one that fell on the day you actually arrived was quieter but revealing. On August 24, 1931, the government of the United Kingdom collapsed under the weight of the Great Depression. Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald — leader of the Labour Party — dissolved his own cabinet and reformed a National Government coalition with the Conservatives and Liberals to manage the financial crisis. His own party expelled him for it. Britain was facing a run on the pound; gold reserves were hemorrhaging; the orthodox remedy was austerity so severe that MacDonald's Labour cabinet had refused to accept it. The child born that Monday arrived on the day one of Britain's major political figures chose his country over his party, and paid for it permanently.

The world that produced this crisis was the world you were born into. The Great Depression had been grinding for nearly two years. American unemployment was approaching twenty percent. Banks were failing across Europe. Germany's banking system had effectively collapsed that summer, and with it, much of whatever political stability the Weimar Republic had managed to assemble. A failed Austrian painter named Adolf Hitler had, in the September 1930 elections, made his party the second largest in the German Reichstag. In August 1931, he was not yet chancellor, not yet inevitable — but he was watching.

**Twenty-five days after your birth** — on September 18, 1931 — Japanese officers of the Kwantung Army staged an explosion on a railway near Mukden in Manchuria and used it as a pretext to invade. The Manchurian Incident was the first domino. From that point, the sequence of events that would produce the Second World War had begun, though no one yet knew the shape of what was coming. The child born in August 1931 spent an entire childhood in the approach to a catastrophe.

You were eight years old when Hitler invaded Poland. You were fourteen when the war ended — when the Nazi regime was exposed in its full enormity, when the atomic bombs fell on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, when the world emerged from six years of industrialized slaughter and tried to understand what had happened to it. The age of nuclear weapons began when you were fourteen years old. It has not ended.

Consider what ninety-five years contains. You were born before radar, before jet aircraft, before commercial television, before penicillin in widespread use. The Empire State Building had been completed three months before your birth; it was the tallest structure in the world and remained so for forty years. You were born in the age of radio, when the intimacy of a president speaking directly to millions of citizens for the first time was still a new thing.

In your lifetime: the New Deal rebuilt American institutions; the Second World War killed an estimated 70 to 85 million people; the United Nations was founded; the Cold War began before you were twenty and ended when you were fifty-eight; a man walked on the Moon when you were thirty-eight; the Berlin Wall fell when you were fifty-eight; the Soviet Union dissolved when you were sixty; the internet remade the world through your sixties and seventies; a global pandemic arrived when you were eighty-eight; and now, at ninety-five, you are present at the beginning of an artificial intelligence revolution that is changing the nature of knowledge itself.

The world of August 24, 1931, held roughly 2.3 billion people. Today there are more than eight billion. Global life expectancy that year was under fifty years. You have nearly doubled it.

The child born on that Depression Monday arrived into a world actively breaking apart — its financial systems failing, its political extremism rising, its empires beginning their long unraveling. The first years of that life were the last years before the catastrophe became undeniable. What followed was reconstruction, and Cold War, and its strange quiet conclusion, and three more transformations since.

The Pompeii that Pliny watched from across the bay was frozen in a single afternoon. The world you were born into has been remade, thoroughly, several times over — and you have been present for all of it.
